title: Musculoskeletal Pharmacology — Session 2

summary.text: Gout runs **purine → uric acid (xanthine oxidase) → urate crystals → neutrophil flare**; treat the **flare** with colchicine, an NSAID, or a corticosteroid, and **never start urate-lowering therapy during a flare**.

**Allopurinol/febuxostat** cut uric acid production (xanthine oxidase), **probenecid** raises excretion (URAT1), and **pegloticase** breaks uric acid down — watch HLA-B*58:01, febuxostat’s CV boxed warning, and G6PD deficiency.
Muscle relaxants sort by site: **central** (baclofen GABA-B, tizanidine α2, cyclobenzaprine brainstem) vs. **peripheral** (**dantrolene** on RyR1 in muscle; botulinum toxin at the junction).

**Dantrolene** is the emergency drug for **malignant hyperthermia**; never stop intrathecal **baclofen** abruptly; check **LFTs** and CYP1A2 inhibitors with tizanidine; cyclobenzaprine is anticholinergic (Beers).

Bone is a **balance**: PTH answers low calcium via bone, kidney, and gut; **bisphosphonates** (first-line), **denosumab**, raloxifene, and calcitonin slow resorption, while **teriparatide/abaloparatide** and **romosozumab** build bone.
Oral bisphosphonates need a **full glass of water, fasting, and 30 minutes upright**; denosumab must not just be stopped, teriparatide is 2 years, and romosozumab carries an MI/stroke boxed warning.

chunks.text: Gout is a crystal-driven inflammatory arthritis with **two very different treatment phases**.

**The chain:** purine metabolism → uric acid → monosodium urate crystals → joint inflammation. Everything downstream — colchicine, allopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid — targets a specific point along this chain.
**Purine breakdown:** hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid (via **xanthine oxidase**) → hyperuricemia → urate crystals in the joint.
Crystals activate neutrophils and macrophages (**NLRP3, IL-1β**) → the acute flare, the end of the cascade.
**Raise urate:** diets rich in purines and fructose; alcohol, especially beer (more production, less renal excretion).
**Lower urate excretion:** diuretics, especially thiazides and loop agents; chronic kidney disease sustains hyperuricemia.

Walk the full chain and sort the drugs into **two buckets:** “lowers uric acid” (allopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid) vs. “treats the acute flare” (colchicine, NSAIDs, corticosteroids) — the same acute-vs-chronic distinction made explicit next.
**Acute flare** — goal: control pain and inflammation now. Agents: colchicine, NSAIDs, corticosteroids.
**Chronic management** — goal: lower serum uric acid to prevent future flares. Agents: allopurinol, febuxostat (↓ production); probenecid (↑ excretion).
Humans lack uricase, the enzyme other mammals use to turn uric acid into soluble allantoin; most people with hyperuricemia never have a gout attack.
Treat gout, not a number: long-term drug treatment of asymptomatic hyperuricemia is unproven. Adherence is poor (18–26% in younger patients).
Colchicine — acute treatment (plant-derived alkaloid, no stem).
Allopurinol — first-line urate-lowering therapy for most patients.
Febuxostat — alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor.
Probenecid — uricosuric (second-line oral). Pegloticase, rasburicase — uricases (refractory).
**Mechanism: disrupts microtubule formation in neutrophils.** Colchicine binds tubulin → less neutrophil migration and NLRP3 activation → less inflammation at the crystal site.
Colchicine works on the cell’s cytoskeleton, so its effect builds in the early hours of a flare.
**Allopurinol** (via its metabolite oxypurinol) and **febuxostat** block **xanthine oxidase** → ↓ uric acid **production**.
Febuxostat is also a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, with a different chemical structure.
**Probenecid — mechanism: inhibits renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid, increasing its excretion** (blocks URAT1). A uricosuric, not a xanthine oxidase inhibitor — a different strategy.
**Pegloticase, rasburicase:** recombinant **uricase** converts uric acid to **allantoin**, which is soluble and excreted.
Uricosurics block reabsorption; uricases remove uric acid enzymatically, which is why they suit refractory disease.
NSAIDs and corticosteroids reduce joint inflammation in a flare.
Allopurinol is a purine analog; its metabolite oxypurinol (half-life 15 hours) also inhibits xanthine oxidase, so it is dosed once daily.
Colchicine relieves gout pain and inflammation in 12–24 hours without changing urate metabolism or excretion.
Glucocorticoids in gout: reduce neutrophil migration, prostaglandins, and IL-1β.
**Treat the acute flare first** (colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid); urate-lowering therapy is deferred until the flare resolves, then used for long-term prevention.
Colchicine is most effective when started early in a flare — **best within 24 hours of onset**.
Allopurinol is first-line for most patients; febuxostat is the alternative when allopurinol is not tolerated or contraindicated.
Probenecid is an older, second-line oral option. **Pegloticase — a recombinant uricase enzyme for severe, refractory gout not controlled by other agents.**
Colchicine flare regimen: 1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg an hour later; prophylaxis 0.6 mg once or twice daily during urate-lowering therapy initiation.
Corticosteroids are a good alternative when NSAIDs or colchicine are contraindicated, including CKD: prednisone 30–50 mg/d for 1–2 days, tapered over 7–10 days, or intra-articular.
All NSAIDs except aspirin, salicylates, and tolmetin treat gout flares.
Febuxostat appears safe in moderate CKD; it can be tried after allopurinol hypersensitivity, though a reaction may still occur.
**Febuxostat: boxed warning for cardiovascular death** — it carries its own cardiovascular safety considerations.
**Colchicine: narrow therapeutic window** — GI adverse effects (diarrhea) are common and dose-limiting.
**Allopurinol:** the **HLA-B*58:01** allele raises the risk of severe hypersensitivity / severe cutaneous reactions.
Pegloticase: infusion reactions are common; anti-drug antibodies can reduce response.
Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (SJS/TEN, fever, eosinophilia, hepatitis, renal failure) usually appears 2–4 weeks after starting — stop at the first rash.
Colchicine can also cause marrow suppression, myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, and neuritis; it is not removed by dialysis.
Febuxostat: liver function abnormalities, diarrhea, headache, nausea.
**Do NOT start urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare** — starting or changing it then can actually prolong the flare. Start or adjust only once the flare has resolved.
**Probenecid:** avoid with a history of uric acid kidney stones or significant renal impairment; needs adequate hydration.
**Pegloticase and rasburicase:** contraindicated in **G6PD deficiency** (hemolysis risk).
Aspirin is avoided in gout: at low doses (≤2.6 g/d) it causes renal retention of uric acid.
Uricosurics should not be used in patients who already excrete large amounts of uric acid.
**Colchicine + CYP3A4 / P-gp inhibitors** (clarithromycin, cyclosporine, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors) → raised levels and toxicity.
**Allopurinol + azathioprine or mercaptopurine:** reduce the dose (xanthine oxidase also clears these drugs).
Allopurinol with azathioprine: cut the azathioprine dose by 75%.
Probenecid also reduces renal secretion of other weak acids, such as penicillin.
Colchicine: adjust the dose for renal or hepatic impairment.
Allopurinol: reduce the dose in renal impairment.
Pegloticase is given by IV infusion.
Allopurinol: start 100 mg/d (≤50 mg/d in CKD), titrate every 2–5 weeks to uric acid <6 mg/dL (max 800 mg/d).
Xanthine oxidase inhibitors: **start low and titrate upward toward a serum urate target**.
When starting urate-lowering therapy, give **colchicine or an NSAID as prophylaxis for 3–6 months**.
Probenecid: keep urine volume high and urine pH above 6.0 early on to prevent stones; start 2–3 weeks after an attack.
Pegloticase: premedicate with a corticosteroid and antihistamine; flares are common in the first 3–6 months.
This acute-vs-chronic distinction is one of the single most testable concepts in gout pharmacology.
Allopurinol vs. febuxostat: both sit on the same enzyme; the choice turns on safety profile and tolerability.
**HLA-B*5801** is a direct callback to Lecture 1’s pharmacogenomics section.
Pegloticase is reserved for refractory cases given its cost, infusion-reaction risk, and need for specialty administration.

Case: sudden, severe pain, redness, and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint — an acute gout flare. **Is this the moment to start acute treatment, chronic urate-lowering therapy, or both?** Acute treatment now; ULT later.
**Name clues:** suffixes often reveal the mechanism before you recall the drug — use them as memory hooks, then confirm each class before prescribing.

**-ostat** marks xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol is the exception); **-ase** names enzymes, so pegloticase and rasburicase are uricases; **-sone, -olone** mark corticosteroids used to treat flares.
Allopurinol already running when a flare hits? Don’t stop it — stopping can worsen and lengthen the attack.
Goal · Acute flare: Control pain and inflammation **now** · Chronic management: Lower serum uric acid to **prevent** future flares

chunks.text: Febuxostat cardiovascular risk: slides say Febuxostat carries a boxed warning for cardiovascular death. Textbook says Initial concerns about increased MACE with febuxostat have not been borne out; the FDA approved only the 40- and 80-mg doses.
Colchicine timing: slides say Best started within 24 hours of flare onset. Textbook says Guidelines suggest giving colchicine within 36 hours of an attack; efficacy falls after that.
Why not start allopurinol in a flare? Shifting urate levels mobilizes crystals — starting or changing ULT during a flare can worsen or prolong it. Calm the flare first.
Why does colchicine have to start early? It works on the neutrophil’s cytoskeleton, stopping migration — once neutrophils have flooded the joint, it has less to prevent.
**Make less, pee more, break it down:** xanthine oxidase inhibitors make less; probenecid pees more; pegloticase breaks it down.
Different mechanisms for **spasm, spasticity, and rigidity** — not the same thing, and they often require distinct pharmacologic approaches.
**Muscle spasm:** sudden, involuntary contraction, often from acute musculoskeletal injury; typically treated with centrally acting relaxants.
**Spasticity:** velocity-dependent increased tone from **upper motor neuron injury**. **Rigidity:** constant increased tone, independent of velocity.

**Where tone is controlled:** upper motor neurons (descending inhibitory pathways) ▸ spinal interneurons (GABA, glycine, alpha-2) ▸ alpha motor neuron ▸ neuromuscular junction (ACh release) ▸ muscle fiber contraction (SR Ca²⁺ release).
**Centrally acting** (act within the CNS to reduce muscle tone): cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, baclofen — first-line; carisoprodol, methocarbamol, metaxalone, chlorzoxazone — other options.

**Peripherally / locally acting:** dantrolene acts directly on skeletal muscle itself; botulinum toxin acts at the neuromuscular junction — useful when a central mechanism is not desired (or not safe).
**Highest-yield distinction:** “where does the drug act?” sorts every agent into one of two buckets — **dantrolene is the only one in the peripheral (muscle) bucket.**
Spasticity is common after spinal injury, cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis, and stroke; these drugs relieve painful spasm better than they restore function.
Baclofen — GABA-B agonist (spinal cord).
Tizanidine — central α2-adrenergic agonist.
Cyclobenzaprine — tricyclic-like central relaxant (brainstem).
Dantrolene — RyR1 blocker in the muscle fiber.
**Central agents** reduce CNS excitatory output to motor neurons → ↓ muscle tone. Baclofen and tizanidine act on spinal interneurons and afferents; cyclobenzaprine acts in the brainstem.

**Baclofen — mechanism: GABA-B receptor agonist in the spinal cord.** Binding GABA-B → opens K⁺ channels, closes Ca²⁺ channels (presynaptic inhibition) → less excitatory transmitter release → lower motor neuron firing → reduced spasticity.
**Tizanidine — mechanism: central α2-adrenergic agonist.** Activating alpha-2 receptors → reduced presynaptic release of excitatory amino acids → lower motor neuron activity → reduced muscle tone.

**Cyclobenzaprine:** acts in the brainstem; antagonizes **5-HT2** and descending serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways → reduced tonic somatic motor activity → muscle relaxation. Structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants.

**Dantrolene — mechanism: decreases calcium release from the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum.** Nerve impulse → DHPR activated → **RyR1** opens → Ca²⁺ released → contraction; dantrolene blocks RyR1 → less Ca²⁺ → relaxation.

chunks.text: Dantrolene acts inside the fiber on RyR1 — directly on the muscle fiber, not the CNS — distinct from every centrally acting agent.

**Botulinum toxin — blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction** (ACh release at the junction) — a third mechanism, distinct from both CNS-acting drugs and dantrolene’s sarcoplasmic-reticulum action.
Diazepam (GABA-A) reduces spasticity partly in the spinal cord, but sedates at the doses needed.
Dantrolene binds RyR1; cardiac and smooth muscle use RyR2, so they are minimally depressed.
**Baclofen:** spasticity, particularly from spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis; intrathecal option for severe spasticity.
Cyclobenzaprine — **primary use: short-term treatment of acute, localized muscle spasm**; short-term use only, 2–3 weeks.

Dantrolene — **clinical use #1: malignant hyperthermia (a true emergency indication)** (triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine) — a true emergency, perioperative indication where the drug is literally life-saving.
**Dantrolene #2:** chronic spasticity, when central agents are not appropriate; also used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome. IV formulation for acute crisis.
**Botulinum toxin:** focal spasticity or dystonia; effect is local and temporary, requiring repeat injections.
Malignant hyperthermia: give IV dantrolene 1 mg/kg, repeated as needed, while controlling acidosis and temperature.
Cyclobenzaprine is ineffective for spasm from cerebral palsy or spinal cord injury.
Gabapentin has shown promise as a spasmolytic in multiple sclerosis.
Botulinum toxin: black box warning for distant spread of toxin, greatest in children treated for spasticity.
**Baclofen:** CNS depression — sedation and weakness, additive risk with other CNS depressants.
**Baclofen withdrawal:** abrupt discontinuation (especially intrathecal) can cause a dangerous syndrome — **seizures, hyperthermia, rebound spasticity**.
**Tizanidine:** sedation, hypotension and bradycardia, dry mouth, **hepatotoxicity**.
**Cyclobenzaprine:** prominent sedation (commonly dosed at night); **anticholinergic** effects — dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion.
**Dantrolene:** hepatotoxicity; generalized weakness.
**Carisoprodol — metabolized to meprobamate; Schedule IV controlled substance with dependence/misuse potential.**
**Chlorzoxazone:** rare but notable hepatotoxicity risk. Methocarbamol is generally less sedating than cyclobenzaprine; metaxalone has a relatively favorable sedation profile.
Tizanidine causes hypotension in 16–33%; abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension and tachycardia.
High-dose baclofen: somnolence, respiratory depression, coma; more seizures in epilepsy.
Carisoprodol withdrawal after long use: anxiety, tremor, twitching, insomnia, hallucinations.
Cyclobenzaprine: use caution in older adults (**Beers list**); MAOIs contraindicated.
Tizanidine with ciprofloxacin or fluvoxamine is contraindicated (CYP1A2).
**Tizanidine + CYP1A2 inhibitors** (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) → strongly raised levels; additive effect with antihypertensives.
**Cyclobenzaprine:** serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol; MAOIs contraindicated.
**Baclofen:** additive sedation with other CNS depressants.
Baclofen: renal dose adjustment.
Tizanidine: start 2 mg every 6–8 hours, max 36 mg/d; adjust for hepatic or renal impairment.
Dantrolene: only about one-third of an oral dose is absorbed; half-life about 8 hours.
Tizanidine requires liver function monitoring (LFTs) with regular use.
Never stop intrathecal baclofen abruptly.
Botulinum toxin injections: no more often than every 3 months.

Name clues: **-curonium / -curium** nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers (vecuronium, atracurium, cisatracurium); **succinylcholine** depolarizing blocker; **-azepam** benzodiazepine (GABA-A, diazepam).

Name clues: **cyclo-** tricyclic-like (cyclobenzaprine); **-idine** central alpha-2 agonist (tizanidine); baclofen has no shared stem (GABA analog); **-trolene** blocks RyR1 (dantrolene); **-toxin** blocks ACh release (botulinum toxin).
Neuromuscular blockers (anesthesia, ICU) paralyze at the end plate and have no CNS activity; succinylcholine is the only depolarizing one.
Succinylcholine can cause fatal hyperkalemia after burns, denervation, or major trauma, and with volatile anesthetics can trigger malignant hyperthermia.
Sugammadex reverses rocuronium/vecuronium; it binds progestins, so use backup contraception for 7 days.
Muscle spasm · What it is: Sudden, involuntary contraction, often after acute injury · Typical approach: Centrally acting relaxant (e.g., cyclobenzaprine, short term)

chunks.text: Why is dantrolene the malignant hyperthermia drug? MH is runaway calcium release through RyR1 in muscle; a CNS drug can’t reach that — dantrolene blocks RyR1 itself.
Why does stopping intrathecal baclofen go badly? The spinal cord loses its GABA-B brake all at once: seizures, hyperthermia, and rebound spasticity.
**Cyclobenzaprine looks like a tricyclic, acts like one:** sleepy, dry, can’t pee, confused — and serotonin syndrome with SSRIs.
Bone pharmacology is about **balancing bone formation and bone resorption**.
**Osteoblasts** build new bone matrix (promoted by several osteoporosis therapies); **osteoclasts** resorb existing bone (suppressed by most osteoporosis therapies).
Nearly every osteoporosis drug shifts this balance one way or the other — slowing osteoclasts or stimulating osteoblasts.
**RANKL/OPG:** osteoblasts or stromal cells express RANKL → RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors → osteoclast differentiation and activation → bone resorption releases calcium.
**OPG** is a decoy receptor that blocks RANKL. Estrogen increases OPG; denosumab mimics OPG. Sclerostin inhibits Wnt signaling in osteoblasts.
**PTH:** intermittent dosing favors formation; continuous exposure raises RANKL and resorption.

**Calcium homeostasis:** PTH raises serum calcium (mobilizes bone calcium when levels drop); vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption; calcitonin lowers serum calcium and opposes PTH; calcium is the substrate being regulated (intake, bone storage, excretion).

**PTH feedback loop:** falling serum calcium → PTH → raises calcium via bone resorption, renal reabsorption, and (via vitamin D activation) intestinal absorption; restored calcium inhibits further PTH.
**Risk factors:** aging; estrogen deficiency (e.g., postmenopausal status); **chronic glucocorticoid use**; low calcium or vitamin D intake; low physical activity.
About 98% of the body’s calcium is in bone; PTH, FGF23, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D are the principal regulators.
Excess endogenous PTH nets bone resorption, but low intermittent doses build bone first — the basis for teriparatide.
Glucocorticoids block vitamin D–driven gut calcium transport, raise renal calcium loss, block formation, and initially stimulate resorption.
Alendronate — oral bisphosphonate (first-line).
Denosumab — RANKL monoclonal antibody.
Teriparatide — PTH analog (anabolic).
Raloxifene — SERM; romosozumab — sclerostin antibody.

Bisphosphonates — **mechanism: inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.** They bind hydroxyapatite at resorption sites → osteoclasts take them up → nitrogen-containing agents inhibit **FPP synthase** (mevalonate pathway) → loss of prenylation of small GTPases → **osteoclast apoptosis**.
**Denosumab:** monoclonal antibody, **RANKL inhibitor** — blocks osteoclast formation.
**Teriparatide** (PTH 1-34, daily injection) / **abaloparatide:** PTH-analog “anabolic” agents that stimulate osteoblasts and new bone formation.
**Romosozumab:** sclerostin antibody that both builds bone and limits resorption — increases formation, decreases resorption → BMD up, fracture risk down.
**SERMs** — selective estrogen receptor modulators (raloxifene): estrogen-like effect on bone — antiresorptive, like calcitonin.
**Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis:** glucocorticoids increase osteoclast-mediated resorption and suppress osteoblast-driven formation.
Amino-bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate) inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway.
Denosumab does not kill osteoclasts and does not deposit in bone, so its effect reverses when stopped.
**Bisphosphonates are first-line for most patients with osteoporosis.**
Higher-risk patients may need an **anabolic agent first**.
Raloxifene also reduces breast cancer risk.
Raloxifene protects against spine fractures but not hip fractures; bisphosphonates, denosumab, and teriparatide protect both.
Vitamin D (800 IU/d) with calcium improves bone density, reduces falls, and prevents fractures — the base under every osteoporosis drug.
Calcitonin is less effective (spine fractures only); bisphosphonates and calcitonin are first-line for Paget disease.
**Romosozumab: boxed warning for MI, stroke, and cardiovascular death.**
Romosozumab: black box — contraindicated after MI or stroke within the past year.
**Bisphosphonates:** esophageal irritation; hypocalcemia; osteonecrosis of the jaw (rare); atypical femoral fractures (rare, with long-term use).
**IV zoledronic acid:** acute-phase reaction (flu-like), mitigated with acetaminophen.
**Raloxifene:** raises VTE risk; hot flashes.
**Denosumab discontinuation causes rebound vertebral fractures** — transition to a bisphosphonate.
Osteonecrosis of the jaw is rare at osteoporosis doses (~1/100,000 patient-years), more common with high-dose IV zoledronate for cancer.
Denosumab: possible infection risk, transient hypocalcemia (CKD, vitamin D deficiency), and rebound resorption if interrupted.
Bisphosphonates: contraindicated with severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30–35 mL/min) — some are avoided in significant renal impairment.
Oral bisphosphonates: avoid in esophageal stricture, achalasia, or inability to sit upright.
Unlike bisphosphonates, denosumab can be used in advanced renal disease (not renally cleared) — watch calcium.
Food, calcium, coffee, and antacids reduce oral bisphosphonate absorption further.
Bisphosphonates have a long skeletal half-life — the effect persists after stopping.
Poor oral absorption (under 1%) → take fasting with plain water.
**Dosing:** alendronate, risedronate — oral, typically weekly; ibandronate — oral, monthly; zoledronic acid — IV, as infrequently as once yearly.
Teriparatide is limited to 2 years lifetime, then follow with an antiresorptive.
Bisphosphonates: less than 10% of an oral dose is absorbed; about half goes to bone, the rest is excreted unchanged in urine.
Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months; teriparatide 20 mcg SC daily; romosozumab 210 mg SC monthly for one year, then an antiresorptive.

**Oral counseling:** take with a **full glass of water**, first thing in the morning, on an empty stomach well before food, and **remain upright** (sitting or standing) for the specified period after dosing (30 minutes).
Ensure calcium and vitamin D repletion before starting; correct hypocalcemia first.
Consider a **drug holiday after 3–5 years** of oral therapy (osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femur fracture with long-term use).
Reassess after 5 years of bisphosphonate (3 for zoledronate); a drug holiday if fracture risk allows.
The “remain upright” point is extremely high-yield: esophageal injury is largely preventable with correct administration.
**Can’t swallow pills?** Yearly IV zoledronic acid or a subcutaneous injectable (e.g., denosumab) avoids the oral route.
Dosing frequency is a major real-world driver of which bisphosphonate a patient actually takes consistently.
Teriparatide, abaloparatide, and romosozumab are the **anabolic exception** — they actively build new bone; most other osteoporosis drugs just slow resorption.
Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis is especially high-yield — it connects to the corticosteroid use for OA/RA in Session 1.

**Choosing therapy:** fracture risk, renal function, previous fracture history, glucocorticoid exposure, adherence (weekly oral vs. yearly IV vs. injectable), and route preference. This checklist is a direct echo of Lecture 1’s clinical decision-making framework.

**1.** Pain and inflammation are related but distinct — treat them accordingly.
**2.** NSAIDs are effective for pain and inflammation, but carry real GI, renal, and cardiovascular risk.
**3.** DMARDs modify the underlying disease process in RA — they do more than mask symptoms.
**4.** Acute gout treatment and chronic urate-lowering therapy are different goals, started at different times.
**5.** Bone pharmacology is fundamentally about the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity.
Every mechanism here — COX inhibition, CYP interactions, renal dosing, pharmacogenomics — is Lecture 1’s toolkit applied to one organ system.
**Patient A — acute gout flare, first presentation:** colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid; check renal/hepatic function and CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (colchicine). No ULT yet.
**Patient B — chronic RA, inadequately controlled:** escalate DMARD therapy (biologic); check infection risk — TB and hepatitis screening first.
**Patient C — osteoarthritis + chronic kidney disease:** acetaminophen or a topical NSAID; avoid oral NSAIDs (renal risk).
**Patient D — postmenopausal osteoporosis, high fracture risk:** consider an anabolic agent first; check its limits (teriparatide 2 years; romosozumab CV boxed warning).

**Recall Q1:** acetaminophen is not a reliable first-line choice for an inflammatory joint flare — it has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory effect; it treats pain and fever, not inflammation itself.
**Recall Q2:** a 70-year-old with CKD and heart failure needing OA pain control — acetaminophen or a topical NSAID avoids the systemic renal/CV risk of oral NSAIDs.
**Recall Q3:** methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase; colchicine disrupts microtubules; baclofen is a GABA-B agonist.
**Recall Q4:** fever on a biologic DMARD — immunosuppression is the shared major risk across all DMARDs; treat a fever as a possible infection until proven otherwise.

**Recall Q5:** probenecid is a uricosuric that inhibits renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid. Colchicine does not lower uric acid; febuxostat (not probenecid) is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor; ULT is deferred during a flare.
**Recall Q6:** glucocorticoids increase osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and suppress osteoblast-driven bone formation — shifting the balance toward bone loss.
Colchicine treats the flare but **does not lower uric acid**; probenecid is **not** a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.
Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist — not a calcium channel blocker in skeletal muscle (that idea belongs to dantrolene’s RyR1 site).

OA in the CKD + anticoagulant + hypertension patient: oral NSAIDs carry the highest combined risk — CKD (renal/AKI risk), anticoagulant (bleeding risk), hypertension (BP/CV risk); acetaminophen or a topical NSAID is generally safer first-line.

When that patient flares with gout: an oral NSAID is still relatively contraindicated; a short corticosteroid course (oral or intra-articular) is often preferred, colchicine needs renal dose adjustment. Defer allopurinol/febuxostat until the flare resolves.

U2-R10.question: Why should urate-lowering therapy never be started or adjusted during an acute gout flare?
U2-R10.answer: Starting/changing ULT during a flare can worsen or prolong it; treat the flare first.

U2-R11.question: What distinguishes a centrally-acting skeletal muscle relaxant from a peripherally-acting one? Which agent is the emergency treatment for malignant hyperthermia, and why?
U2-R11.answer: Central agents reduce CNS excitatory output to motor neurons; dantrolene acts peripherally by decreasing sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release — the emergency drug for malignant hyperthermia.

U2-R12.question: Describe the basic PTH feedback loop in calcium homeostasis: what triggers PTH release, and what three actions does PTH take to raise serum calcium?
U2-R12.answer: Falling calcium triggers PTH, which raises calcium via bone resorption, renal reabsorption, and (indirectly, via vitamin D activation) intestinal absorption.

U2-R13.question: What patient counseling point reduces the risk of esophageal irritation with oral bisphosphonates?
U2-R13.answer: Full glass of water, remain upright — reduces esophageal contact time/irritation.

U2-S.question:
A 72-year-old patient with osteoarthritis also has chronic kidney disease, hypertension, and is taking a chronic anticoagulant. Two months later, the same patient develops sudden, severe pain, redness, and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, consistent with an acute gout flare.
For the osteoarthritis pain, is an oral NSAID a good first-line choice for this patient? Walk through each of this patient's risk factors and what it specifically contraindicates.
For the new acute gout flare, which agents would you consider for immediate symptom control, and which would you specifically avoid given this patient's existing risk factors?
Is this the right visit to start allopurinol or febuxostat? Why or why not, and when would you start it?
U2-S.answer: Oral NSAIDs carry the highest combined risk here — CKD (renal/AKI risk), anticoagulant (bleeding risk), hypertension (BP/CV risk); acetaminophen or a topical NSAID is generally safer first-line. For the acute flare, an oral NSAID is still relatively contraindicated given the same risk factors — a short corticosteroid course (oral or intra-articular) is often preferred, and colchicine would need renal dose adjustment. Defer allopurinol/febuxostat until the flare resolves.

quiz.stem: In Figure 4, probenecid and allopurinol both lower serum uric acid, but through different mechanisms. What is the key difference?

tree.name: Part 1 · Gout: Acute Flares & Urate-Lowering Therapy

children.name: Class
facts: Gout is a crystal-driven inflammatory arthritis with **two very different treatment phases**.

**The chain:** purine metabolism → uric acid → monosodium urate crystals → joint inflammation. Everything downstream — colchicine, allopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid — targets a specific point along this chain.
**Purine breakdown:** hypoxanthine → xanthine → uric acid (via **xanthine oxidase**) → hyperuricemia → urate crystals in the joint.
Crystals activate neutrophils and macrophages (**NLRP3, IL-1β**) → the acute flare, the end of the cascade.
**Raise urate:** diets rich in purines and fructose; alcohol, especially beer (more production, less renal excretion).
**Lower urate excretion:** diuretics, especially thiazides and loop agents; chronic kidney disease sustains hyperuricemia.

Walk the full chain and sort the drugs into **two buckets:** “lowers uric acid” (allopurinol, febuxostat, probenecid) vs. “treats the acute flare” (colchicine, NSAIDs, corticosteroids) — the same acute-vs-chronic distinction made explicit next.
**Acute flare** — goal: control pain and inflammation now. Agents: colchicine, NSAIDs, corticosteroids.
**Chronic management** — goal: lower serum uric acid to prevent future flares. Agents: allopurinol, febuxostat (↓ production); probenecid (↑ excretion).
Humans lack uricase, the enzyme other mammals use to turn uric acid into soluble allantoin; most people with hyperuricemia never have a gout attack.
Treat gout, not a number: long-term drug treatment of asymptomatic hyperuricemia is unproven. Adherence is poor (18–26% in younger patients).

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Colchicine — acute treatment (plant-derived alkaloid, no stem).
Allopurinol — first-line urate-lowering therapy for most patients.
Febuxostat — alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor.
Probenecid — uricosuric (second-line oral). Pegloticase, rasburicase — uricases (refractory).

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Mechanism: disrupts microtubule formation in neutrophils.** Colchicine binds tubulin → less neutrophil migration and NLRP3 activation → less inflammation at the crystal site.
Colchicine works on the cell’s cytoskeleton, so its effect builds in the early hours of a flare.
**Allopurinol** (via its metabolite oxypurinol) and **febuxostat** block **xanthine oxidase** → ↓ uric acid **production**.
Febuxostat is also a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, with a different chemical structure.
**Probenecid — mechanism: inhibits renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid, increasing its excretion** (blocks URAT1). A uricosuric, not a xanthine oxidase inhibitor — a different strategy.
**Pegloticase, rasburicase:** recombinant **uricase** converts uric acid to **allantoin**, which is soluble and excreted.
Uricosurics block reabsorption; uricases remove uric acid enzymatically, which is why they suit refractory disease.
NSAIDs and corticosteroids reduce joint inflammation in a flare.
Allopurinol is a purine analog; its metabolite oxypurinol (half-life 15 hours) also inhibits xanthine oxidase, so it is dosed once daily.
Colchicine relieves gout pain and inflammation in 12–24 hours without changing urate metabolism or excretion.
Glucocorticoids in gout: reduce neutrophil migration, prostaglandins, and IL-1β.

children.name: Indications
facts: **Treat the acute flare first** (colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid); urate-lowering therapy is deferred until the flare resolves, then used for long-term prevention.
Colchicine is most effective when started early in a flare — **best within 24 hours of onset**.
Allopurinol is first-line for most patients; febuxostat is the alternative when allopurinol is not tolerated or contraindicated.
Probenecid is an older, second-line oral option. **Pegloticase — a recombinant uricase enzyme for severe, refractory gout not controlled by other agents.**
Colchicine flare regimen: 1.2 mg, then 0.6 mg an hour later; prophylaxis 0.6 mg once or twice daily during urate-lowering therapy initiation.
Corticosteroids are a good alternative when NSAIDs or colchicine are contraindicated, including CKD: prednisone 30–50 mg/d for 1–2 days, tapered over 7–10 days, or intra-articular.
All NSAIDs except aspirin, salicylates, and tolmetin treat gout flares.
Febuxostat appears safe in moderate CKD; it can be tried after allopurinol hypersensitivity, though a reaction may still occur.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Febuxostat: boxed warning for cardiovascular death** — it carries its own cardiovascular safety considerations.
**Colchicine: narrow therapeutic window** — GI adverse effects (diarrhea) are common and dose-limiting.
**Allopurinol:** the **HLA-B*58:01** allele raises the risk of severe hypersensitivity / severe cutaneous reactions.
Pegloticase: infusion reactions are common; anti-drug antibodies can reduce response.
Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (SJS/TEN, fever, eosinophilia, hepatitis, renal failure) usually appears 2–4 weeks after starting — stop at the first rash.
Colchicine can also cause marrow suppression, myopathy, rhabdomyolysis, and neuritis; it is not removed by dialysis.
Febuxostat: liver function abnormalities, diarrhea, headache, nausea.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: **Do NOT start urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare** — starting or changing it then can actually prolong the flare. Start or adjust only once the flare has resolved.
**Probenecid:** avoid with a history of uric acid kidney stones or significant renal impairment; needs adequate hydration.
**Pegloticase and rasburicase:** contraindicated in **G6PD deficiency** (hemolysis risk).
Aspirin is avoided in gout: at low doses (≤2.6 g/d) it causes renal retention of uric acid.
Uricosurics should not be used in patients who already excrete large amounts of uric acid.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Colchicine + CYP3A4 / P-gp inhibitors** (clarithromycin, cyclosporine, strong CYP3A4 inhibitors) → raised levels and toxicity.
**Allopurinol + azathioprine or mercaptopurine:** reduce the dose (xanthine oxidase also clears these drugs).
Allopurinol with azathioprine: cut the azathioprine dose by 75%.
Probenecid also reduces renal secretion of other weak acids, such as penicillin.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Colchicine: adjust the dose for renal or hepatic impairment.
Allopurinol: reduce the dose in renal impairment.
Pegloticase is given by IV infusion.
Allopurinol: start 100 mg/d (≤50 mg/d in CKD), titrate every 2–5 weeks to uric acid <6 mg/dL (max 800 mg/d).

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors: **start low and titrate upward toward a serum urate target**.
When starting urate-lowering therapy, give **colchicine or an NSAID as prophylaxis for 3–6 months**.
Probenecid: keep urine volume high and urine pH above 6.0 early on to prevent stones; start 2–3 weeks after an attack.
Pegloticase: premedicate with a corticosteroid and antihistamine; flares are common in the first 3–6 months.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: This acute-vs-chronic distinction is one of the single most testable concepts in gout pharmacology.
Allopurinol vs. febuxostat: both sit on the same enzyme; the choice turns on safety profile and tolerability.
**HLA-B*5801** is a direct callback to Lecture 1’s pharmacogenomics section.
Pegloticase is reserved for refractory cases given its cost, infusion-reaction risk, and need for specialty administration.

Case: sudden, severe pain, redness, and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint — an acute gout flare. **Is this the moment to start acute treatment, chronic urate-lowering therapy, or both?** Acute treatment now; ULT later.
**Name clues:** suffixes often reveal the mechanism before you recall the drug — use them as memory hooks, then confirm each class before prescribing.

**-ostat** marks xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol is the exception); **-ase** names enzymes, so pegloticase and rasburicase are uricases; **-sone, -olone** mark corticosteroids used to treat flares.
Allopurinol already running when a flare hits? Don’t stop it — stopping can worsen and lengthen the attack.

children.name: Class
facts: Different mechanisms for **spasm, spasticity, and rigidity** — not the same thing, and they often require distinct pharmacologic approaches.
**Muscle spasm:** sudden, involuntary contraction, often from acute musculoskeletal injury; typically treated with centrally acting relaxants.
**Spasticity:** velocity-dependent increased tone from **upper motor neuron injury**. **Rigidity:** constant increased tone, independent of velocity.

**Where tone is controlled:** upper motor neurons (descending inhibitory pathways) ▸ spinal interneurons (GABA, glycine, alpha-2) ▸ alpha motor neuron ▸ neuromuscular junction (ACh release) ▸ muscle fiber contraction (SR Ca²⁺ release).
**Centrally acting** (act within the CNS to reduce muscle tone): cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, baclofen — first-line; carisoprodol, methocarbamol, metaxalone, chlorzoxazone — other options.

**Peripherally / locally acting:** dantrolene acts directly on skeletal muscle itself; botulinum toxin acts at the neuromuscular junction — useful when a central mechanism is not desired (or not safe).
**Highest-yield distinction:** “where does the drug act?” sorts every agent into one of two buckets — **dantrolene is the only one in the peripheral (muscle) bucket.**
Spasticity is common after spinal injury, cerebral palsy, multiple sclerosis, and stroke; these drugs relieve painful spasm better than they restore function.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Baclofen — GABA-B agonist (spinal cord).
Tizanidine — central α2-adrenergic agonist.
Cyclobenzaprine — tricyclic-like central relaxant (brainstem).
Dantrolene — RyR1 blocker in the muscle fiber.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: **Central agents** reduce CNS excitatory output to motor neurons → ↓ muscle tone. Baclofen and tizanidine act on spinal interneurons and afferents; cyclobenzaprine acts in the brainstem.

**Baclofen — mechanism: GABA-B receptor agonist in the spinal cord.** Binding GABA-B → opens K⁺ channels, closes Ca²⁺ channels (presynaptic inhibition) → less excitatory transmitter release → lower motor neuron firing → reduced spasticity.
**Tizanidine — mechanism: central α2-adrenergic agonist.** Activating alpha-2 receptors → reduced presynaptic release of excitatory amino acids → lower motor neuron activity → reduced muscle tone.

**Cyclobenzaprine:** acts in the brainstem; antagonizes **5-HT2** and descending serotonergic and noradrenergic pathways → reduced tonic somatic motor activity → muscle relaxation. Structurally related to tricyclic antidepressants.

**Dantrolene — mechanism: decreases calcium release from the skeletal muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum.** Nerve impulse → DHPR activated → **RyR1** opens → Ca²⁺ released → contraction; dantrolene blocks RyR1 → less Ca²⁺ → relaxation.
Dantrolene acts inside the fiber on RyR1 — directly on the muscle fiber, not the CNS — distinct from every centrally acting agent.

**Botulinum toxin — blocks presynaptic acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction** (ACh release at the junction) — a third mechanism, distinct from both CNS-acting drugs and dantrolene’s sarcoplasmic-reticulum action.
Diazepam (GABA-A) reduces spasticity partly in the spinal cord, but sedates at the doses needed.
Dantrolene binds RyR1; cardiac and smooth muscle use RyR2, so they are minimally depressed.

children.name: Indications
facts: **Baclofen:** spasticity, particularly from spinal cord injury or multiple sclerosis; intrathecal option for severe spasticity.
Cyclobenzaprine — **primary use: short-term treatment of acute, localized muscle spasm**; short-term use only, 2–3 weeks.

Dantrolene — **clinical use #1: malignant hyperthermia (a true emergency indication)** (triggered by volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine) — a true emergency, perioperative indication where the drug is literally life-saving.
**Dantrolene #2:** chronic spasticity, when central agents are not appropriate; also used for neuroleptic malignant syndrome. IV formulation for acute crisis.
**Botulinum toxin:** focal spasticity or dystonia; effect is local and temporary, requiring repeat injections.
Malignant hyperthermia: give IV dantrolene 1 mg/kg, repeated as needed, while controlling acidosis and temperature.
Cyclobenzaprine is ineffective for spasm from cerebral palsy or spinal cord injury.
Gabapentin has shown promise as a spasmolytic in multiple sclerosis.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: Botulinum toxin: black box warning for distant spread of toxin, greatest in children treated for spasticity.
**Baclofen:** CNS depression — sedation and weakness, additive risk with other CNS depressants.
**Baclofen withdrawal:** abrupt discontinuation (especially intrathecal) can cause a dangerous syndrome — **seizures, hyperthermia, rebound spasticity**.
**Tizanidine:** sedation, hypotension and bradycardia, dry mouth, **hepatotoxicity**.
**Cyclobenzaprine:** prominent sedation (commonly dosed at night); **anticholinergic** effects — dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, confusion.
**Dantrolene:** hepatotoxicity; generalized weakness.
**Carisoprodol — metabolized to meprobamate; Schedule IV controlled substance with dependence/misuse potential.**
**Chlorzoxazone:** rare but notable hepatotoxicity risk. Methocarbamol is generally less sedating than cyclobenzaprine; metaxalone has a relatively favorable sedation profile.
Tizanidine causes hypotension in 16–33%; abrupt withdrawal causes rebound hypertension and tachycardia.
High-dose baclofen: somnolence, respiratory depression, coma; more seizures in epilepsy.
Carisoprodol withdrawal after long use: anxiety, tremor, twitching, insomnia, hallucinations.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Cyclobenzaprine: use caution in older adults (**Beers list**); MAOIs contraindicated.
Tizanidine with ciprofloxacin or fluvoxamine is contraindicated (CYP1A2).

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: **Tizanidine + CYP1A2 inhibitors** (ciprofloxacin, fluvoxamine) → strongly raised levels; additive effect with antihypertensives.
**Cyclobenzaprine:** serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol; MAOIs contraindicated.
**Baclofen:** additive sedation with other CNS depressants.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Baclofen: renal dose adjustment.
Tizanidine: start 2 mg every 6–8 hours, max 36 mg/d; adjust for hepatic or renal impairment.
Dantrolene: only about one-third of an oral dose is absorbed; half-life about 8 hours.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: Tizanidine requires liver function monitoring (LFTs) with regular use.
Never stop intrathecal baclofen abruptly.
Botulinum toxin injections: no more often than every 3 months.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: Name clues: **-curonium / -curium** nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers (vecuronium, atracurium, cisatracurium); **succinylcholine** depolarizing blocker; **-azepam** benzodiazepine (GABA-A, diazepam).

Name clues: **cyclo-** tricyclic-like (cyclobenzaprine); **-idine** central alpha-2 agonist (tizanidine); baclofen has no shared stem (GABA analog); **-trolene** blocks RyR1 (dantrolene); **-toxin** blocks ACh release (botulinum toxin).
Neuromuscular blockers (anesthesia, ICU) paralyze at the end plate and have no CNS activity; succinylcholine is the only depolarizing one.
Succinylcholine can cause fatal hyperkalemia after burns, denervation, or major trauma, and with volatile anesthetics can trigger malignant hyperthermia.
Sugammadex reverses rocuronium/vecuronium; it binds progestins, so use backup contraception for 7 days.

children.name: Class
facts: Bone pharmacology is about **balancing bone formation and bone resorption**.
**Osteoblasts** build new bone matrix (promoted by several osteoporosis therapies); **osteoclasts** resorb existing bone (suppressed by most osteoporosis therapies).
Nearly every osteoporosis drug shifts this balance one way or the other — slowing osteoclasts or stimulating osteoblasts.
**RANKL/OPG:** osteoblasts or stromal cells express RANKL → RANKL binds RANK on osteoclast precursors → osteoclast differentiation and activation → bone resorption releases calcium.
**OPG** is a decoy receptor that blocks RANKL. Estrogen increases OPG; denosumab mimics OPG. Sclerostin inhibits Wnt signaling in osteoblasts.
**PTH:** intermittent dosing favors formation; continuous exposure raises RANKL and resorption.

**Calcium homeostasis:** PTH raises serum calcium (mobilizes bone calcium when levels drop); vitamin D increases intestinal calcium absorption; calcitonin lowers serum calcium and opposes PTH; calcium is the substrate being regulated (intake, bone storage, excretion).

**PTH feedback loop:** falling serum calcium → PTH → raises calcium via bone resorption, renal reabsorption, and (via vitamin D activation) intestinal absorption; restored calcium inhibits further PTH.
**Risk factors:** aging; estrogen deficiency (e.g., postmenopausal status); **chronic glucocorticoid use**; low calcium or vitamin D intake; low physical activity.
About 98% of the body’s calcium is in bone; PTH, FGF23, and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D are the principal regulators.
Excess endogenous PTH nets bone resorption, but low intermittent doses build bone first — the basis for teriparatide.
Glucocorticoids block vitamin D–driven gut calcium transport, raise renal calcium loss, block formation, and initially stimulate resorption.

children.name: Prototype + other drugs named
facts: Alendronate — oral bisphosphonate (first-line).
Denosumab — RANKL monoclonal antibody.
Teriparatide — PTH analog (anabolic).
Raloxifene — SERM; romosozumab — sclerostin antibody.

children.name: Mechanism of action
facts: Bisphosphonates — **mechanism: inhibit osteoclast-mediated bone resorption.** They bind hydroxyapatite at resorption sites → osteoclasts take them up → nitrogen-containing agents inhibit **FPP synthase** (mevalonate pathway) → loss of prenylation of small GTPases → **osteoclast apoptosis**.
**Denosumab:** monoclonal antibody, **RANKL inhibitor** — blocks osteoclast formation.
**Teriparatide** (PTH 1-34, daily injection) / **abaloparatide:** PTH-analog “anabolic” agents that stimulate osteoblasts and new bone formation.
**Romosozumab:** sclerostin antibody that both builds bone and limits resorption — increases formation, decreases resorption → BMD up, fracture risk down.
**SERMs** — selective estrogen receptor modulators (raloxifene): estrogen-like effect on bone — antiresorptive, like calcitonin.
**Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis:** glucocorticoids increase osteoclast-mediated resorption and suppress osteoblast-driven formation.
Amino-bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate) inhibit farnesyl pyrophosphate synthase in the mevalonate pathway.
Denosumab does not kill osteoclasts and does not deposit in bone, so its effect reverses when stopped.

children.name: Indications
facts: **Bisphosphonates are first-line for most patients with osteoporosis.**
Higher-risk patients may need an **anabolic agent first**.
Raloxifene also reduces breast cancer risk.
Raloxifene protects against spine fractures but not hip fractures; bisphosphonates, denosumab, and teriparatide protect both.
Vitamin D (800 IU/d) with calcium improves bone density, reduces falls, and prevents fractures — the base under every osteoporosis drug.
Calcitonin is less effective (spine fractures only); bisphosphonates and calcitonin are first-line for Paget disease.

children.name: Adverse effects (boxed warnings first)
facts: **Romosozumab: boxed warning for MI, stroke, and cardiovascular death.**
Romosozumab: black box — contraindicated after MI or stroke within the past year.
**Bisphosphonates:** esophageal irritation; hypocalcemia; osteonecrosis of the jaw (rare); atypical femoral fractures (rare, with long-term use).
**IV zoledronic acid:** acute-phase reaction (flu-like), mitigated with acetaminophen.
**Raloxifene:** raises VTE risk; hot flashes.
**Denosumab discontinuation causes rebound vertebral fractures** — transition to a bisphosphonate.
Osteonecrosis of the jaw is rare at osteoporosis doses (~1/100,000 patient-years), more common with high-dose IV zoledronate for cancer.
Denosumab: possible infection risk, transient hypocalcemia (CKD, vitamin D deficiency), and rebound resorption if interrupted.

children.name: Contraindications
facts: Bisphosphonates: contraindicated with severe renal impairment (CrCl below 30–35 mL/min) — some are avoided in significant renal impairment.
Oral bisphosphonates: avoid in esophageal stricture, achalasia, or inability to sit upright.
Unlike bisphosphonates, denosumab can be used in advanced renal disease (not renally cleared) — watch calcium.

children.name: Drug interactions
facts: Food, calcium, coffee, and antacids reduce oral bisphosphonate absorption further.

children.name: Pharmacokinetics
facts: Bisphosphonates have a long skeletal half-life — the effect persists after stopping.
Poor oral absorption (under 1%) → take fasting with plain water.
**Dosing:** alendronate, risedronate — oral, typically weekly; ibandronate — oral, monthly; zoledronic acid — IV, as infrequently as once yearly.
Teriparatide is limited to 2 years lifetime, then follow with an antiresorptive.
Bisphosphonates: less than 10% of an oral dose is absorbed; about half goes to bone, the rest is excreted unchanged in urine.
Denosumab 60 mg SC every 6 months; teriparatide 20 mcg SC daily; romosozumab 210 mg SC monthly for one year, then an antiresorptive.

children.name: Monitoring
facts: **Oral counseling:** take with a **full glass of water**, first thing in the morning, on an empty stomach well before food, and **remain upright** (sitting or standing) for the specified period after dosing (30 minutes).
Ensure calcium and vitamin D repletion before starting; correct hypocalcemia first.
Consider a **drug holiday after 3–5 years** of oral therapy (osteonecrosis of the jaw, atypical femur fracture with long-term use).
Reassess after 5 years of bisphosphonate (3 for zoledronate); a drug holiday if fracture risk allows.

children.name: Clinical pearls / "why" hook
facts: The “remain upright” point is extremely high-yield: esophageal injury is largely preventable with correct administration.
**Can’t swallow pills?** Yearly IV zoledronic acid or a subcutaneous injectable (e.g., denosumab) avoids the oral route.
Dosing frequency is a major real-world driver of which bisphosphonate a patient actually takes consistently.
Teriparatide, abaloparatide, and romosozumab are the **anabolic exception** — they actively build new bone; most other osteoporosis drugs just slow resorption.
Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis is especially high-yield — it connects to the corticosteroid use for OA/RA in Session 1.

**Choosing therapy:** fracture risk, renal function, previous fracture history, glucocorticoid exposure, adherence (weekly oral vs. yearly IV vs. injectable), and route preference. This checklist is a direct echo of Lecture 1’s clinical decision-making framework.

Name clues: **-dronate** bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid = zoledronate); **-sumab** bone monoclonal antibodies (denosumab RANKL, romosozumab sclerostin); **-fene** SERM (raloxifene); **-tide** PTH analogs (teriparatide, abaloparatide); calcitonin has no shared stem (hormone).

tree.name: Part 4 · Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit

children.name: Key definitions
facts: Applying the whole musculoskeletal pharmacology toolkit: for each patient, name a first-line drug class AND the single biggest safety concern to check before prescribing it.

children.name: How it works
facts: **1.** Pain and inflammation are related but distinct — treat them accordingly.
**2.** NSAIDs are effective for pain and inflammation, but carry real GI, renal, and cardiovascular risk.
**3.** DMARDs modify the underlying disease process in RA — they do more than mask symptoms.
**4.** Acute gout treatment and chronic urate-lowering therapy are different goals, started at different times.
**5.** Bone pharmacology is fundamentally about the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity.
Every mechanism here — COX inhibition, CYP interactions, renal dosing, pharmacogenomics — is Lecture 1’s toolkit applied to one organ system.

children.name: Clinical relevance
facts: **Patient A — acute gout flare, first presentation:** colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid; check renal/hepatic function and CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors (colchicine). No ULT yet.
**Patient B — chronic RA, inadequately controlled:** escalate DMARD therapy (biologic); check infection risk — TB and hepatitis screening first.
**Patient C — osteoarthritis + chronic kidney disease:** acetaminophen or a topical NSAID; avoid oral NSAIDs (renal risk).
**Patient D — postmenopausal osteoporosis, high fracture risk:** consider an anabolic agent first; check its limits (teriparatide 2 years; romosozumab CV boxed warning).

children.name: Drugs named as examples
facts: **Recall Q1:** acetaminophen is not a reliable first-line choice for an inflammatory joint flare — it has minimal peripheral anti-inflammatory effect; it treats pain and fever, not inflammation itself.
**Recall Q2:** a 70-year-old with CKD and heart failure needing OA pain control — acetaminophen or a topical NSAID avoids the systemic renal/CV risk of oral NSAIDs.
**Recall Q3:** methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase; colchicine disrupts microtubules; baclofen is a GABA-B agonist.
**Recall Q4:** fever on a biologic DMARD — immunosuppression is the shared major risk across all DMARDs; treat a fever as a possible infection until proven otherwise.

**Recall Q5:** probenecid is a uricosuric that inhibits renal tubular reabsorption of uric acid. Colchicine does not lower uric acid; febuxostat (not probenecid) is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor; ULT is deferred during a flare.
**Recall Q6:** glucocorticoids increase osteoclast-mediated bone resorption and suppress osteoblast-driven bone formation — shifting the balance toward bone loss.

children.name: Exam traps
facts: Colchicine treats the flare but **does not lower uric acid**; probenecid is **not** a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.
Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist — not a calcium channel blocker in skeletal muscle (that idea belongs to dantrolene’s RyR1 site).

OA in the CKD + anticoagulant + hypertension patient: oral NSAIDs carry the highest combined risk — CKD (renal/AKI risk), anticoagulant (bleeding risk), hypertension (BP/CV risk); acetaminophen or a topical NSAID is generally safer first-line.

When that patient flares with gout: an oral NSAID is still relatively contraindicated; a short corticosteroid course (oral or intra-articular) is often preferred, colchicine needs renal dose adjustment. Defer allopurinol/febuxostat until the flare resolves.

brief.part: Part 1 · Gout: Acute Flares & Urate-Lowering Therapy
hy: Acute gout treatment and chronic urate-lowering therapy are different goals, started at different times.
Flare: colchicine, NSAID, or corticosteroid. Prevention: allopurinol/febuxostat (↓ production) or probenecid (↑ excretion).
Colchicine: microtubules; best within 24 h; diarrhea; CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitors.
Allopurinol: HLA-B*58:01; febuxostat: boxed CV death warning.
Central (cyclobenzaprine, tizanidine, baclofen) vs. peripheral (dantrolene — muscle; botulinum — junction).
Dantrolene blocks RyR1 SR Ca²⁺ release → malignant hyperthermia.
Baclofen: GABA-B; never stop intrathecal abruptly.
Bone pharmacology is fundamentally about the balance between osteoblast and osteoclast activity.
PTH: falling calcium → bone resorption, renal reabsorption, vitamin D–mediated gut absorption.
Bisphosphonates first-line; full glass of water, upright 30 minutes.
Denosumab = RANKL antibody; stopping → rebound vertebral fractures.

brief.part: Part 4 · Putting It All Together: Musculoskeletal Toolkit
hy: Five takeaways: pain ≠ inflammation; NSAIDs = GI/renal/CV risk; DMARDs change RA; gout = acute vs. chronic; bone = osteoblast vs. osteoclast.
traps: Colchicine treats the flare but **does not lower uric acid**; probenecid is **not** a xanthine oxidase inhibitor.
Baclofen is a GABA-B agonist — not a calcium channel blocker in skeletal muscle (that idea belongs to dantrolene’s RyR1 site).

OA in the CKD + anticoagulant + hypertension patient: oral NSAIDs carry the highest combined risk — CKD (renal/AKI risk), anticoagulant (bleeding risk), hypertension (BP/CV risk); acetaminophen or a topical NSAID is generally safer first-line.

When that patient flares with gout: an oral NSAID is still relatively contraindicated; a short corticosteroid course (oral or intra-articular) is often preferred, colchicine needs renal dose adjustment. Defer allopurinol/febuxostat until the flare resolves.
